findings.title: Migration/compat story fully satisfies the plan's explicit requirement
findings.description: The plan entry requires "a defined migration/compat story for projects that already committed personal keys … into an existing shared `.context-forge.toml`." The design delivers a three-part story that is complete without being overweight: (1) read-time fallback so a personal key still sitting in the shared file keeps resolving (compat, no silent regression), (2) a new `ConsistencyChecker` rule that surfaces the stale shared-file copy as a `warning` so the condition is discoverable rather than silent, and (3) a dedicated, idempotent `cf config migrate-personal` command that performs the explicit, reviewable move. The collision semantics (absent-in-personal → move; different-value → skip-and-report; identical → dedupe) and the write-personal-then-delete-shared ordering with per-key failure isolation are specified concretely, not left as "TBD." A lighter interpretation (fallback-only with no detection or command) would leave the migration requirement under-specified, so the added mechanisms are justified by a named requirement.

findings.title: Proportionality — new file-routing extends the existing merge pattern rather than inventing one
findings.description: The plan instructs the slice to route reads/writes "reusing the existing user-vs-project two-file-precedence merge pattern rather than inventing a new one." The design honors this: it reuses the existing `readToml`/`writeToml`/`resolveKey`/`setKey`/`deleteKey` helpers unchanged, preserves file-not-found-means-empty semantics, and extends the precedence to `project-personal → project-shared → user → default` by inserting one more-specific layer governed by the same "more specific scope wins" principle — not by building a new resolution engine. The `.context-forge.local.toml` sibling file is the lightest option that actually solves the gitignore problem (a `[personal]` table inside one file was correctly rejected because a file cannot be half-gitignored). The `scope` field is made required with no default so future keys force an explicit classification at review time, which is a cheap compile-time guard rather than added runtime mechanism. The `cf init` gitignore addition is correctly limited to the one line this feature needs, with the broader template deferred to the plan's Future Work item.

findings.title: Failure modes enumerated for each new I/O path
findings.description: For the new `.context-forge.local.toml` write path, the design states `ConfigManager.set` reuses the existing `writeToml` helper so write failures (permission, disk full) throw exactly as for the existing files — no new error-handling path. For `migrate-personal`, it enumerates permission-denied / disk-full / TOML-serialization failures, specifies the write-personal-then-delete-shared ordering that leaves keys present-in-both on partial failure, states idempotent re-runnability, and requires per-key continue-on-failure with `failed: <error>` reporting rather than whole-run abort. For `cf init`'s gitignore append, it specifies the file read-modify-write failure path surfaces through the existing `handleError`. None are left implicit.

findings.title: "916 prerequisite fix" label is non-load-bearing but potentially confusing
findings.description: The design refers to "the 916 prerequisite fix (already merged to main) established `--project`/`--global` as the CLI's explicit scope-selection flags." Per the parent slice plan, entry 916 is "Guide Update Branch Guard" — a different concern — so the attribution is not obvious to reconcile. This does not affect correctness: the design's actual load-bearing assumption is only that the `--project`/`--global` flags already exist, which the plan entry for 915 itself confirms (`cf config set --project` is described as existing behavior), and the slice explicitly states it does not change that CLI surface. Flagging only so a reviewer does not waste time trying to map the prerequisite onto 916's actual scope.
